content: Miliary tuberculosis is a specific form of tuberculosis characterized by widespread dissemination of the infection throughout the body. The lesions associated with this condition are very small, typically measuring between 1 to 5 millimeters in size. The term miliary is derived from the appearance of these lesions on a chest X-ray, where they resemble millet seeds scattered across the lung fields. This form of tuberculosis can affect multiple organs, including the lungs, liver, and spleen. It is considered a complication that occurs in approximately 1-3% of all tuberculosis cases. The pathophysiology of tuberculosis begins when an individual inhales airborne droplets containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis. These droplets are expelled into the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Once inhaled, the bacteria can establish small areas of infection in the lungs, known as granulomas, which are localized collections of immune cells attempting to contain the infection. Disseminated tuberculosis, or miliary tuberculosis, develops in individuals whose immune systems fail to effectively contain the initial infection. This can occur within weeks of the primary infection or, in some cases, years later. The risk of developing miliary tuberculosis is significantly higher in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with AIDS or those taking immunosuppressive medications. Infants and elderly individuals are also at an increased risk due to their relatively weaker immune defenses. Patients with miliary tuberculosis often present with non-specific symptoms, which can make diagnosis challenging. Common symptoms include a low-grade fever, persistent cough, and generalized lymphadenopathy (enlarged lymph nodes). In some cases, patients may also exhibit hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) in approximately 40% of cases, splenomegaly (enlarged spleen) in about 15% of cases, and, less commonly, pancreatitis in fewer than 5% of cases. Severe cases may involve multiorgan dysfunction, including adrenal insufficiency. Tuberculosis is a preventable disease, even for individuals who have been exposed to an infected person. Early detection and treatment are critical in preventing the progression and complications of the disease.
